narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance was documented in 1841 within Frederick Hill's Book of Quadrilles and Country Dances.
While the original manuscript recorded a version in 3/2 time, the version practiced today is a modern composition.
It is categorized as a Scottish National dance, a subset of the broader Highland dancing tradition.

narration: The dance serves as a technical benchmark in the Scottish Highland dance system, used specifically for medal testing and competitive performance.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to pipe marches.
Common tunes include 'The Barren Rocks of Aden', 'Braes of Mar', and 'Scotland the Brave'.
Listen for the Great Highland Bagpipe.
The pulse is 2/4 or 4/4.

The sound is defined by the steady, driving drone and melodic piercing of the Great Highland Bagpipe playing traditional marches. The rhythm is square and precise, suitable for the sharp footwork of Highland dance.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear the standard Highland dance costume, consisting of a kilt and waistcoat.
This is notable because female dancers do not wear the Aboyne dress usually required for National dances.
It is performed on stages for competitions and medal testing.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Frederick Hill is the primary historical figure associated with the dance, having recorded it in his 1841 manuscript.
The sources distinguish between the 1841 'Hill version' in 3/2 time and the 'modern composition' performed today.
It is a subclass of Scottish Highland dance and a member of the 'National dance' subtype.
